extracted.intended_audience: members of Congress, patent stakeholders (companies, universities, inventors), patent practitioners and policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the substantive provisions and policy tradeoffs in H.R. 1908 (Patent Reform Act of 2007), describing how the bill would change venue, damages, post-grant review, priority rules, willfulness, prior-user rights, and PTO oversight. Intended to inform legislative debate and stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue / forum shopping reform
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill will allow cases to be filed where the defendant is located or has committed acts relevant to the patent dispute; it restores balance by allowing cases to be brought in locales including where the defendant is incorporated or has its principal place of business or has committed a substantial portion of the acts of infringement and has a physical facility controlled by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to remove glaring instances of forum shopping by patent trolls. Freest rules are given to independent inventors and universities; corporate plaintiffs can only bring cases where the facilities are located if they have engaged in activities relevant to the patent dispute. Debate noted controversial earlier language that would have allowed transfer only to districts where the defendant had 'substantial evidence or witnesses' and raised concerns about judges being unable to consider fairness, caseloads, delays, or small-entity hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-inventor-to-file priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: H.R. 1908 converts the U.S. patent system from a first-to-invent system to a first-inventor-to-file system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A grace period is maintained to reduce negative impact on small inventors and universities. The bill requires periodic review (PTO study every seven years) of the effects of revisions made to the derivation litigation system to monitor long-term effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for calculating fair and equitable remedies (damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 provides a formula to ensure that the patent owner is rewarded for the actual value of the patented invention and clarifies that courts may use multiple methods to compute damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computing damages is complex (illustrated by the turbine blade hypothetical). Apportionment was originally susceptible to being required in all cases, but as amended 'apportionment is only one of the several methods a court can use in awarding damages,' including the current Georgia-Pacific approach. Apportionment no longer applies to damages based on lost profits. The bill allows recovery of the enhanced value of previously known elements where their combination adds value or functionality. The PTO Director must study effectiveness of section 5 every seven years and report recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement standard and good-faith defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may only find willful infringement if the patent owner shows, by clear and convincing evidence, that (1) the infringer, after receiving detailed written notice from the patentee, performed the acts of infringement, (2) the infringer intentionally copied the patented invention with knowledge that it was patented, or (3) after having been found by a court to have infringed a patent, the infringer engaged in conduct that again infringed on the same patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An allegation of willfulness is subject to a 'good faith' defense. The provision narrows and clarifies when willfulness can be found to limit arbitrary enhancement of damages for willful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of prior user rights defense
rubrics_metrics.description: H.R. 1908 expands the 'prior user rights' defense to infringement, protecting earlier inventors who began using a product or process (although unpatented) before another obtained a patent for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a defensive option for commercial users who had prior use, balancing patent owner rights and established commercial actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review and re-examination reform
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill cures principal deficiencies of re-examination and creates a new post-grant review providing an effective and efficient system for challenging patent validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: a single opportunity for challenge that must be initiated within 12 months of the patent being granted; PTO Director must prescribe rules for abuse of discovery or improper use of the proceeding; limits on the types of prior art which may be considered; and a prohibition on a party reasserting claims in court that it raised in post-grant review. These measures are intended to prevent abuse of the proceeding and to make administrative review more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeals and claim-construction clarity (Markman orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: H.R. 1908 provides the Federal Circuit jurisdiction over interlocutory decisions (Markman orders) in which the district court construes the claims of a patent as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to clarify claim scope early in litigation and make patent litigation more efficient by enabling appellate review of claim construction before final judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special protections for independent inventors and universities
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill gives the freest rules to independent inventors and to individual inventors and universities, noting their special role in the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative text and debate emphasize preserving opportunities for small inventors (including 'working out of a garage'), and balancing reforms so as not to harm small entities, universities, and the innovation ecosystem dependent on licensing and commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO oversight and mandatory periodic studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill requires the PTO Director (Undersecretary for Intellectual Property) to conduct studies and submit reports on the effects of major changes (e.g., derivation litigation changes and section 5 damages changes) at the end of a seven-year period and every seven years thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mandated studies are intended to monitor long-term effects, identify unforeseen negative consequences, and recommend amendments or other mechanisms to Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on reassertion of issues and discovery abuse in administrative proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill prohibits a party from reasserting claims in court that it raised in post-grant review and requires the PTO to prescribe rules for abuse of discovery or improper use of the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aimed at preventing tactical or abusive serial litigation (claim-splitting) and overbroad discovery in administrative challenges, thereby protecting patent owners from repeated attacks while allowing a meaningful administrative check on patent validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of varied damages methodologies (including Georgia-Pacific factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill preserves the use of the current approach established in Georgia-Pacific v. United States Plywood Corp. (reasonable royalty as what the infringer would have paid and patent owner would have accepted) as one of the methods available to courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While introducing a formula and emphasizing apportionment as a method, the bill explicitly allows courts to continue to use established case-law approaches to determine reasonable royalties, ensuring continuity with precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern about comprehensive reform vs. narrow fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative debate raises the evaluative principle that some patent problems (e.g., 'patent trolls') might be better addressed by limited, narrowly tailored changes rather than sweeping, comprehensive reform that could have unintended consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers recommend cautious, incremental changes (e.g., restricting the ability of secondary holders to sue) as alternatives to wholesale revision, invoking the 'do no harm' principle when altering longstanding patent law.
